articles.title: Banks are back online, but the outages could leave customers vulnerable to scams
articles.summary: Customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, U.S. Bank and other major financial institutions reported service outages on Monday, according to Downdetector.com . Other banks that saw a spike in customer complaints about difficulty accessing their accounts included Capital One, Truist and Wells Fargo, while users also reported problems with the digital payments app Zelle, according to the outage tracker. However, Downdetector showed that service was back to normal at the banks and Zelle early Tuesday. CBS News has reached out for comment to Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Capital One. Chase Bank's services were experiencing a technical bug issue, not a cyber issue, a spokesperson said Monday. "Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds," a Chase spokesperson said in a statement. "We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible." Chase also said in a social media post that a software bug in its systems affected other institutions "when we were party to a transaction involving other banks." The issue is not systemic, the bank added. "Please try back later" Some Chase customers received a message that said, "Some services aren't available. We're working on them. Please try back later." Bank customers started reporting problems accessing online services on Monday morning. By the afternoon, reports of outages had surged, according to Downdetector.com. As of 2 p.m. ET, nearly 4,800 users had reported problems with Chase, the most of any bank. Chase customers reported issues accessing their online accounts, including viewing balances and performing transactions such as bank transfers and wire transfers, according to Downdetector. Bank of America clients reported problems with ATMs as well as online and mobile banking services, according to the outage tracker. A Bank of America spokesperson told CBS News its "systems have been operating normally today." U.S. Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app. They also had problems transferring funds, while Wells Fargo customers reported difficulty signing in to their accounts, as well as with getting account balances and conducting transactions. A Chase Bank customer in Texas told CBS News he tried to deposit a check at a Dallas branch early Monday, but the transaction could not be completed. A bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" without providing additional details, he added, expressing frustration at the lack of clarity about the situation. A spokesperson for U.S. Bank said its systems were not directly impacted by the cyber outage. "However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays," the company said in a statement to CBS News. A Capital One spokesperson said it hasn't been affected by the outage and continues to operate normally. Zelle told CBS News its service was "operating as it should," but that some users could be experiencing issues related to problems at their financial institutions, which could be delaying Zelle payments. "Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds," a Zelle spokesperson said. "Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds." Zelle's network operator, Early Warning Services, is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo. 3 tech crises highlight fragile systems The banking outages occurred after Microsoft restored services on Saturday following a global outage affecting its Outlook and Teams services, which disrupted users, companies and government operations worldwide. Microsoft said a technical issue caused the outage and that it was not linked to a cyberattack. The glitches also came only days after overloaded routers forced the Federal Aviation Administration to order a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday, stranding travelers and causing thousands of canceled flights. The FAA said Sunday that airline schedules across the U.S. were returning to normal . (On Monday evening, United Airlines also said it resolved a " widespread system outage " it had been dealing with that afternoon.) Cybersecurity experts said the root causes of the bank service disruptions, Microsoft outage and FAA system failure, while different on their face, also point to a common problem. "Our country has seen three very serious technology incidents over the past week," Mike Chapple, an IT, analytics and operations expert at the University of Notre Dame, said in a statement to CBS News. "When we dig into the details, each one has an explanation that makes sense on its own, but they all point to a common theme: the complexity and fragility of the systems that we depend on every day." He noted that in each case, a technical issue quickly rippled through interconnected systems, causing massive disruptions nationwide. "We don't yet know much about today's banking system outage, but it appears to stem from a technical issue at Chase that affected other banks through their shared payment networks," Chapple added. When big companies like JPMorgan Chase experience technical disruptions, their impact often reverberates industrywide, added Karen Panetta, dean of graduate engineering at Tufts University. "The larger companies have global reach that affords their customers flexibility and seamless integration with other businesses," she told CBS News. "Unfortunately, when one of these backbone providers has disruptions, the downstream effects are magnified. The multiple entities that rely on those services are also affected." What should bank customers do? Kayne McGladrey, a security expert and senior member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, said bank customers might have better luck going to their local branch in person, noting that financial services often still work on site when online banking resources go down. "Try ATMs, cards, phone banking and branches, which often keep working when the app doesn't," she said in a statement to CBS News. She also advised people to keep records of any attempted or failed transactions. "Screenshot failed transactions and error messages, since you may need them for reconciliation or fee waivers. Once service is back, ask the bank to reverse any fees the outage caused," McGladrey said. She also urged consumers to ignore unsolicited emails about the bank outages, which she warned might be phishing scams. Instead, people should rely on their bank's official communication channels for information, McGladrey said. Craig Timm, senior director of anti-money laundering at ACAMS, an anti-financial-crime organization, told CBS News he expects criminals to exploit consumer anxiety about potentially losing access to their money, and that consumers should "assume they will be targeted." That's in part because AI lets scammers act fast and at scale. Timm said common tactics to be alert to include criminals exerting pressure on targets "to take urgent action to protect their funds or restore account access." "These scams may take the form of fake bank alerts, phishing texts or emails, or social media posts that claim to offer help," he said. "Some schemes aim to steal banking login credentials, while others use malicious links to gain access to a victim's computer." articles.title: Trump-Kim Jong Un reunion looks more likely after unexpected signal from Russia
articles.summary: By Brenda Goh and Joyce Lee SEOUL, Nov 17 (Reuters) - The odds of US President Donald Trump meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on the sidelines of the APEC summit have gone up after the Kremlin said a meeting between Kim and Russian President Vladimir Putin was possible, analysts said. Trump has ‌repeatedly expressed interest in meeting Kim again and said on Monday it might happen in China this week. However, previously mooted meetings have not taken place and US and South ‌Korean officials have said the chances were low. But a report by Russia's Interfax news agency quoting the Kremlin saying Putin could meet Kim if the North Korean leader attended this week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen has shifted bets. The ​Kremlin "wouldn't do that unless they were certain he was going to meet," said Sydney Seiler, a former US national intelligence officer for North Korea, now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. "I'm pretty confident something's underway." A series of visits by North Korean officials to Russia and China in recent weeks, as well as by Russian and Chinese delegations to Pyongyang, could also have been for summit preparations. Kim also made a surprise visit to the Chinese border city of Dandong last month. "There's been these little signs," said John Delury, a professor at the Hopkins-Nanjing Center. "If Kim goes to Shenzhen, he's going ‌to talk to Donald Trump." Trump said the North Korean leader's presence ⁠at APEC was ultimately up to Chinese President Xi Jinping. China as the host country is able to invite non-APEC members for informal talks on the sidelines but the organisation's members would need to be consulted. China's Foreign Ministry, the North Korean embassy in Beijing and APEC did not ⁠immediately respond to requests for comment. PYONGYANG'S DEMANDS Trump's interest in renewed engagement with Kim comes seven years after their last summit ended without agreement over curtailing North Korea's nuclear weapons and sanctions relief. North Korea has repeatedly signalled it unwilling to resume discussions unless denuclearisation is off the agenda. Trump has referred to North Korea as a nuclear power, a status allies in the region and the West have refused to ​recognise. Seiler ​said a meeting would likely be more symbolic than substantive but could be a step for Kim to ​push for North Korea to be recognised internationally as a nuclear ‌state. "It's not going to happen overnight, but eventually (Kim) hopes to wear down the world to accept North Korea as a nuclear power," he said. For Trump, "you have the meeting simply to build the relationship." Others remain sceptical about a meeting coming to fruition. There is little sign that China is making preparations for Kim to travel and Trump made similar comments before he left for APEC meeting in South Korea last year, a person familiar with the situation said. There was nothing to gain for Kim to go except photo opportunities, said Kim Dong-yup, a professor at Kyungnam University's Far East Institute. "Let's say they offer to remove sanctions. But sanctions are already not working. There's nothing to gain for Kim. Why would he go and open himself ‌up to potential uncertainty?" The Kremlin's remarks are less about US-North Korea relations and more bluster to show ​Russia has influence over North Korea, he added. MULTILATERAL EVENTS ATTENDANCE RARE Kim's last appearance at a multilateral event was in ​September last year, a military parade in Beijing attended by more than two ​dozen national leaders, including Putin. North Korean state media announced Kim's participation days before and he travelled to Beijing in an armoured train Delury said he expected ‌Kim, if he did attend APEC, to travel via an Air China ​plane to Shenzhen as he did when he ​visited Singapore in 2018 for the first of his two summits with Trump during the US president's first term. South Korea and Japan have also been closely watching the possibility of a Trump-Kim meeting and both countries' leaders will be at APEC. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has said he hopes Trump can persuade Kim to resume ​dialogue. South Korea's Unification Ministry said it had nothing to confirm ‌when asked about Kim's possible trip to Shenzhen. Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has repeatedly sought a summit with Kim Jong Un to resolve the long-running issue ​of Japanese nationals abducted by North Korea in the 1970s and 1980s. Pyongyang has rebuffed Tokyo's approaches. (Reporting by Brenda Goh and Joyce Lee in Seoul; Additional ​reporting by John Geddie in Tokyo and Ju-min Park in Shenzhen; editing by Lincoln Feast.) articles.title: Nvidia dismisses 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign as Trump backs effort to reinstate ex-CEO
articles.summary: Donald Trump greeting Jensen Huang in September this year [Getty Images] Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort. Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign. But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs , including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy. The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia. The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance. Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted. Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return. The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive. They expressed concerns the firm's co-founder "was removed without meaningful due process". Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back. Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of the affair but resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him. The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times , though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him. A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report. The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House. Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy". Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company. The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy. It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley [Reuters] New rules The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which have been allegedly used as a way for Chinese firms to gain access to advanced chips to train AI models. The move comes ahead of a meeting this week between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping , whose countries are locked in a race to lead AI development. The interim rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to prevent them from being illegally diverted to China. The measure is designed to ensure existing restrictions on sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Department of Commerce said. Huang has been a vocal advocate for easing chip export restrictions on China, arguing that broad access to global markets is crucial for the competitiveness of the US. He said in 2025 that the market for AI chips in China would eventually reach $50bn - a sum Huang said "is like Boeing - not a plane - the entire company". In 2025, Nvidia won an approval to sell some advanced AI chips in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington. How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security? How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House The ex-Nvidia boss' affair with Alice Huang, the former director of a Singaporean data centre firm called Megaspeed, has raised the level of scrutiny over deals abroad . The small South East Asian business hub has been a draw for companies all around the world, many of which have set up headquarters in Singapore. Major US firms like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have set up offices in the business-friendly country, alongside Chinese companies like TikTok-owner ByteDance and Tencent. But Singapore's openness to business has also made it the ideal address to place orders for restricted advanced semiconductors. Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the chip giant earns. But notably, only 2% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, which acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere. While Singapore does not necessarily prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to  companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls. Advanced semiconductors, crucial for the development of AI models, are at the centre of the US and China's technological rivalry. US officials have long viewed the country's technological supremacy as a matter of national security and have expressed concerns that sharing the best chips could give China's economy and military a boost. Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair. Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said. The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump. 'A handshake with Jensen' Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation. "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X. "Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost." Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question." But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine". Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm. Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading. In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang". Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation. For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday. articles.title: White House's $50 billion air traffic demand hits GOP turbulence in Senate
articles.summary: Top Senate Republicans are all but ruling out immediate approval for the Trump administration’s plea for $50 billion to help overhaul the nation’s aging air traffic control system. Majority Leader John Thune indicated Monday that he won’t seek to muscle the money through Congress using a Republican-only reconciliation bill — despite calls by President Donald Trump and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy for quick action following last week’s hourslong ground stop due to a malfunction of critical aviation communication infrastructure. Instead, Thune raised the prospect of negotiating the funding with Democrats, some of whom are expressing skepticism about the Trump administration’s modernization effort. “We’re looking at what the needs are and doing that assessment, and then we’ll figure out what we can or are able to do and whether we can find bipartisan support to do something,” Thune told reporters at the Capitol. “That’s always key.” He later said he would prefer to tackle the matter through the “normal” appropriations process, adding: “The question is: Are we going to partner with the Democrats?” Democrats, though, don’t appear to be itching to rapidly OK the $50 billion — an amount that Duffy unveiled Friday hours after air travel came to a halt across the country. Days earlier, Duffy had said the administration was pushing for $30 billion . In a speech on the Senate floor Monday, Minority Leader Chuck Schumer decried the Trump administration’s response to the ground stop, while adding that DOT had barely spent the $12.5 billion that Congress had provided in last year’s GOP megalaw. “We want to give them all the money they need, but they’ve got to use it, and know how to implement it — and they don’t,” he said. Other Democrats on Monday offered similar remarks. 'I don't see the justification' Even some Republicans expressed skepticism at the dollar amount. “I don’t see the justification yet for that much,” Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine) said of the $50 billion, adding that she would need more detail on the request. She also noted that much of the $12.5 billion remains unspent. Despite the rumblings from Capitol Hill, the Transportation Department continued to push for the money. “The American people are in agreement that the country needs to invest in a Brand New Air Traffic System today,” DOT spokesperson Danna Almeida told POLITICO in a statement. On Monday, Trump said he didn’t take any responsibility for the ground stop, blaming the Biden administration, while adding that the air traffic control system “had a heart attack.” On Sunday, he wrote on Truth Social : “We need Congress to give the money, FAST!” He added in another post that the overhaul “should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs.” In an appearance on Fox News on Monday night, Vice President JD Vance reinforced that message: “This is not an expensive problem ... we need to reinvest and rebuild that infrastructure.” Federal Aviation Administration chief Bryan Bedford and Duffy have said the failure was likely caused, in part, by a botched installation of a router at an air traffic control telecommunications facility, which government contractor L3Harris oversees. Duffy will be on Capitol Hill on Tuesday to make his case to Republicans at a regular GOP weekly lunch. He spoke to Speaker Mike Johnson on Monday, said a person familiar with the conversation, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. The DOT chief was key in securing the $12.5 billion funding in last year’s Republican megalaw, which is aimed at modernizing the nation’s aging and stressed air traffic control system. But Duffy has continued to push Congress for additional dollars, saying he needs more to finish the job. Thune told reporters Monday that extra money is necessary but also noted that funding in the reconciliation law “hasn’t been used yet.” According to FAA data shared with Congress and reviewed by POLITICO, the agency as of Oct. 31 has legally committed $4.3 billion — roughly 35% — of the 2025 Republican reconciliation law’s air traffic control money. It has spent just over $1 billion, or about 9%, the data shows. Seeking clarity Other Republicans echoed Thune, saying that any funding should come out of the appropriations process, not via reconciliation. Whether that would be part of a year-end omnibus bill or stand-alone legislation wasn’t immediately clear. But it would mean Republicans could not push it through the Senate without Democratic cooperation, avoiding a filibuster. Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), a member of the Senate Commerce Committee, said he wasn't in favor of using reconciliation to pass the funding. “This is an issue that affects all Americans,” he said Monday. “I do not wanna do it through reconciliation.” Moreno also said he needed clarity on how DOT came up with the $50 billion figure. “What they need to do is give Congress one number that’s very, very thought out, that’s defendable, that’s accurate,” he said. “And then Congress should pass that immediately.” Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), when asked if he supports Duffy’s $50 billion request, said: “I think we need to get him some more money. It doesn’t need to come out of reconciliation.” Instead, he said, it should be from the appropriations process. Republicans are already mulling Trump’s recent request for $350 billion in a reconciliation bill for the Defense Department. Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) introduced legislation in September to get Duffy around $30 billion, though a major chunk of that funding would be for airports. DOT earlier this week touted that it has swapped out 70% of copper telecommunications lines across dozens of facilities for more modern technologies, among other accomplishments during the overhaul. Similar to Schumer’s remarks, the Senate Appropriations Committee’s top Democrat, Sen. Patty Murray of Washington state, said Monday the administration hasn’t “spent the money that they’re sitting on” and she has received “no justification” for the ask. “I want to know where the money’s going to go [and] what they’re doing with the current allocation,” Murray said. And Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), an appropriator and the anticipated majority whip next Congress, said, “I generally support the idea of investing in air traffic control, but $50 billion sounds like an awfully round number.” Jordain Carney, Chris Marquette, Mia McCarthy and Oriana Pawlyk contributed to this report. articles.title: FAA, Microsoft, banks: Why it feels like everything keeps breaking
articles.summary: From grounded flights to frozen bank accounts , why does it seem like everything is breaking at once? First, millions of people lost access to their email . Next, the nation's skies went quiet. Then, a wave of customers trying to send money through Zelle were met with error messages. In just five days, a rapid succession of high-profile technology failures has left consumers rattled. The Federal Aviation Administration was forced into a rare nationwide ground stop. Microsoft’s ubiquitous office software went dark. Now a software bug has hit banking, and United Airlines had a fleeting system outage that delayed flight departures. Public anxiety coursed through social media. "So are we just pretending like it's normal that all of the mainstream banks are down today? After Microsoft? And planes? And..." one TikToker posted. "Can y'all wake me up when this timeline is over?" added another. The good news: No sign of a cyberattack First, the reassuring news. Patrick Moorhead, founder of Moor Insights and Strategy, says there is no evidence of a coordinated cyberattack and "nothing is falling apart." Instead, these compounding outages highlight a deeper structural vulnerability: How heavily our critical infrastructure relies on highly concentrated systems. "When one piece fails, it fails at national scale," Moorhead said. Modern technological systems are so complex and tightly interwoven that a single error can snowball instantly, wiping out essential services, according to Mike Chapple, a professor at the University of Notre Dame. The FAA outage, for example, was triggered by either a faulty component or an installation error by a government contractor during a modernization project. That single mistake flooded the air traffic control network with data, crippling nationwide infrastructure, Chapple said. Meanwhile, the Microsoft outage was caused by a dormant software bug that had lingered undetected since July. Last week, "conditions were just right to activate the bug, triggering a cascade of failures that knocked thousands of systems offline and hindered repair efforts," he said. While the exact cause of the banking disruptions remains unclear, Chapple speculated it is likely a technical issue in shared payment networks. Chase said it experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug. The catch? Routine changes cause massive ripples American consumers are right to be frustrated, said Daniel Newman, CEO of Futurum Group. "Increasingly, there is a lack of clarity to consumers around why outages are happening and how they are being remedied," Newman said. Any vulnerability in these crucial systems is cause for major concern, says Mitch Ashley, vice president and practice lead at the Futurum Group. "Daily life runs on a small number of systems and a failure in one now reaches millions of people at once," he said. What's more, the recent spate of incidents while unrelated point to a common issue, said Virginia Tech professor Ali Butt. A "routine change" set each one off, he said. "Microsoft’s outage has been linked to a network configuration change and the FAA ground stop was traced to a maintenance upgrade on a single router. Imagine that, a single component in a sea of thousands or more components," Butt said. "In tightly connected systems, a small change made without fully mapping its downstream effects can spread far beyond where it started." Will outages get worse? Likely The bad news is that our dependence on massive-scale technology is only growing. Experts warn we should expect these failures to happen more often and hit harder. "Should people panic? No. Should we ask for better engineering? Yes," Butt said. "That means testing changes for their downstream impact, rolling them out in stages, isolating faults and setting clear policies for systems the public depends on." articles.title: Ex-Commerce Dept. staffers say there was a lack of enforcement under Lutnick
articles.summary: Some former Commerce Department officials are describing Howard Lutnick's tenure as secretary as being marked by "chaos," "micromanaging," and what they allege are failures to act on evidence of highly sensitive computer chip smuggling. A key national security responsibility of the department is investigating and enforcing bans on the export to China and other U.S. adversaries of advanced computer chips used in artificial intelligence and sophisticated weapons. "There was an inexplicable refusal to use the tools at their disposal for national security over the last year," one former Commerce official told CBS News. Scrutiny of Lutnick's tenure has heightened in recent days with Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO after admitting an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies believed to be a Chinese spy. China has denied the accusation of spying, calling it "an attempt to smear China." As the scandal has unfolded, senior officials and members of Congress have questioned how Nvidia was permitted to sell chips to companies with deep ties to China, and whether the Commerce Department policed those exports effectively. The answer, according to some of Lutnick's former staff, was not at all. Four ex-Commerce officials spoke with CBS News, asking to remain anonymous, fearing professional reprisals for discussing their recent experience in government. "We weren't able to add entities to the Entity List. That was just a complete stop," one former Commerce employee said, referring to the federal list of firms that the U.S. government has banned from buying the most advanced chips due to the belief they would route them to China or other adversaries. Another former Commerce official said a whole year passed with no companies added to the list, noting that this was the first time that had happened in 18 years. The Federal Register shows the last time entities were added was Oct. 9, 2025, and the last yearlong gap in additions was in 2008. The first former staffer said the agency's own enforcement officers found suspicious activity at Southeast Asian sites where Nvidia chips had been delivered, but that Commerce directors allegedly took no action. Placement on the list triggers more stringent license requirements and creates a higher threshold to prevent sensitive products from getting where they shouldn't, the ex-official said. Instead, "nothing happened," the ex-official said. The Biden administration issued AI chip export controls in 2022 and 2023, and in January 2025 issued an interim final rule to block China and other adversaries from obtaining the most advanced AI chips, both directly and through third-party countries. In May 2025, President Trump's Commerce Department rolled back the rule, arguing it "would have stifled American innovation." Instead, the department said it would strengthen export controls for AI chips by issuing guidance to the industry and public. There are growing signs that bans on exporting advanced U.S. computer chips have been circumvented in large quantities, according to published reports. An April 2026 study by AI research nonprofit Epoch estimated between 290,000 and 1.6 million cutting-edge AI chips were smuggled into China in 2024 and 2025, comprising "roughly a quarter of the comput[ing power] China acquired through legal channels or domestic production." Tech news site The Information reported that at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips allegedly ended up with Chinese companies since 2023 just through companies linked to Alice Huang , the suspected Chinese agent accused of an affair with Nvidia's ousted CEO. The report cited sources close to her for the estimate. And a former researcher at OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, published a paper last week claiming to have found digital forensic evidence that top Chinese AI models were trained using Nvidia chips banned in China. One former Commerce staffer described the department under Lutnick as "very chaotic, very frantic," with staff sometimes learning of major policy changes via media reports, including a pivot to allow the sale of Nvidia's H20 and H200 chips to China — the company's second-most advanced tier of GPUs. "We found out about that in The New York Times," the ex-Commerce official said. "It was pretty clear that the decision was made between Trump and Jensen Huang." The Commerce Department did not respond to a request for comment.  CBS News has also reached out to the White House for comment. On Monday the department imposed a new rule requiring licenses for exporting, re-exporting or transferring advanced semiconductors to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore or Thailand, aimed at closing a loophole through which chips were exported to China via an intermediary. But the Commerce Department suggested that its own involvement was limited, describing the rule as "written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council—to address remote access to advanced super intelligence (SI) chips and servers." The department lost two of its most senior and experienced experts shortly after Lutnick took office. One was Matthew Borman, who served as principal deputy assistant secretary for export administration. Borman had been with the department for over 30 years. Another veteran official, Eileen Albanese, was let go from her longtime role as director of the Office of National Security Controls. Reuters first reported their departures in February 2025, the same month Lutnick started running the department. "They kicked off the administration by essentially firing the two most respected people," said one former employee. A profile on the website of law firm Akin Gump, where Albanese now works, says she played a "key role in the development of U.S. export control policy and regulations for advanced artificial intelligence chips and semiconductor manufacturing tools." "Matt and Eileen were treasures of the U.S. government," one former Commerce staffer said. Albanese did not respond to a request for comment. Borman declined to comment. Former officials said subsequent changes under Lutnick helped prompt an "exodus" of up to 50 skilled staff members over the past 18 months. Over time, those who departed were among the most experienced officials who dealt with key areas including chips and export control enforcement, the ex-staffers said. "It was an exodus of the finest engineers and scientists, the key experts on AI, on Russia, on diversion, our key expert on chips. Decades of institutional memory and skill went out," an ex-employee said. Key roles remain vacant in Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, the department in charge of export controls, according to a registry of current senior federal employees. The principal deputy assistant secretary for export administration, the same role for export enforcement and the chief of staff roles are all currently unfilled, the records say. Some staff described a bottleneck at the Bureau of Industry and Security, accusing its chief — Jeffrey Kessler, a top deputy to Lutnick — of "micromanaging" and blocking enforcement against companies suspected of smuggling chips. "He made everything go through him. Literally every possible decision, the most minor things. It's impossible for one person to manage that level of things," one former employee under Lutnick told CBS News. "He didn't want to make any decisions on his own. He would want you to make a memo and he would say, 'Package it up with options for me to bring to a decision maker,' which always cracked me up. Because it's like, who are you? A concerned citizen?" "The career workforce felt frustrated and stymied," said one former staffer from the previous administration, who is close to many who remained in the department. "They felt like they were unable to do their jobs because [Kessler and Lutnick] were standing in their way." The former staff members told CBS News that the critical view of Lutnick and his deputy was widely shared in the department. Cabinet members have even voiced criticism, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessen t telling CNBC last week that Lutnick failed to follow through on chip ban enforcement supported by Treasury, the State Department and others in the administration. "Commerce has the pen. You would have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told the channel. "I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above" a certain sophistication, Bessent said. articles.title: FEMA will test a nationwide emergency alert on Tuesday. Your phone won't get it.
articles.summary: Be forewarned: Today, TVs and radios — not wireless phones — nationwide will blare a jolting emergency alert. But don't be alarmed; it's only a test. We repeat: It's only a test. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), along with the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), is running it to ensure the Emergency Alert System (EAS) for radio and television works during an actual emergency, such as a natural disaster, terrorist attack or other threat to public safety. Wireless phones will not receive the test alert. "Wireless Emergency Alerts were tested in 2023, but they will not be part of this year's test," according to FEMA. It comes amid online conspiracy theories that there will be a 90-day power outage starting Tuesday, which only intensified after last week's Microsoft global Outlook outage and the Federal Aviation Administration's rare ground stop. The federal government has not announced a nationwide 90-day blackout or plans to shut down the U.S. power grid. The rumors are centered around a Pentagon plan to ensure the military has access to critical energy, infrastructure and other resources in case of future disruptions. FEMA quashed any rumors in an X post on Monday, saying, "We've heard a lot of rumors about tomorrow's EAS test. Let's clear things up. It lasts 1 minute, and no action is required. No blackouts, no secret emergencies." We’ve heard a lot of rumors about tomorrow’s EAS test. 📺📻 Let’s clear things up. It lasts 1 minute, and no action is required. No blackouts, no secret emergencies. Just our legally mandated, routine test on TV and radio at approximately 2:20 PM ET: https://t.co/WGD7xCuRDB pic.twitter.com/HEErLQVKga — FEMA (@fema) November 16, 2026 Here's what you can expect and what to know about the FEMA test today. When will the alert test happen? Here's when you can expect to be alerted depending on your time zone: 2:20 p.m. ET 1:20 p.m. CT 12:20 p.m. MT 11:20 a.m. PT 10:20 a.m. AT 9:20 a.m. HT What will the test look and sound like? Radio and television broadcasters nationwide will interrupt their programming with a message that generally says: "This is a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System, issued by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. This is only a test. No action is required by the public." According to FEMA , the Emergency Alert System involves thousands of independently operated radio, television, cable, satellite and wireline broadband providers. Since they use different equipment, the visual or audio formats may differ by station. "The test will include alert tones to support accessibility for individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing," according to FEMA. And depending on the broadcaster and their capabilities, the message will be delivered in English, Spanish or both. How long will the test last? If your TV or radio is on and tuned to a broadcast station, cable system, satellite radio or television provider, or wireline video service, you should receive the test from the EAS, which is expected to take about one minute. Why is the national emergency test happening? Federal law requires FEMA to test the Integrated Public Alert and Warning System (IPAWS) at least once every three years. The last national test was conducted on Oct. 4, 2023. "If an actual emergency or significant weather event occurs on test day, FEMA and the FCC may postpone the test," according to FEMA . "The backup date for the nationwide test is December 3, 2026." articles.title: 'Everybody's shell-shocked': GOP insiders face 2028 prospects after midterm defeats
articles.summary: On Election Day, many Republicans were bracing for a tough outcome, but not what has been described as a blue tsunami. "I thought that we were going to keep the Senate," former Republican National Committee Chair Ronna McDaniel told ABC News. "I didn't think that Democrats could make inroads in states like South Carolina and Kansas and even Texas." Joe Raedle/Getty Images - PHOTO: RNC Chairwoman Ronna McDaniel delivers remarks before the NBC News Republican Presidential Primary Debate, Nov. 8, 2023, in Miami. Democrats did more than make inroads. They flipped eight GOP-held Senate seats and as of Monday, Democrats hold 256 House seats to the GOP's 170. There are still some outstanding races as of Monday: nine House races and one Senate race. Over a dozen Republican donors and operatives told ABC News that the Republican Party is still in shock after the sweeping midterm losses. They pointed to a message that focused on culture wars and failed to reach voters squeezed by costs tied to the war in Iran and a Latino coalition that slipped away. Some argued Vice President JD Vance may no longer be the presumptive 2028 nominee. Vance, who has not formally announced he is launching a presidential bid for 2028, has acknowledged "there's a chance" he won't run in 2028. 'The South is in play': Longtime red states emerge as potential battleground for Democrats The president’s record- low approval ratings were also difficult to ignore, some said. "The losses are all about Trump," said one Republican consultant who worked on races out West and spoke to ABC News on the condition of anonymity. "This was a total rebuke of Donald Trump, both him personally and his politics." RNC National Press Secretary Natalie Baldassarre said in a statement that Republicans will "continue to put America first,” highlighting that the RNC raised $130 million, sending more than $60 million directly to Republican campaigns. When reached for comment, the White House emphasized Trump’s signature tax legislation and said that Trump will continue to work for the American people. "Under President Trump’s leadership, this administration has signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, secured the border, cut the cost of prescription drugs, added more than one million private-sector jobs, and locked in nearly 20 trade deals. President Trump will never stop delivering results for the American people and he will undoubtedly go down as the most successful and consequential president in American history," White House spokesman Davis Ingle told ABC News in a statement. Vance's office, when asked for comment, deferred to the White House. A m ess a ging p roble m The donors and operatives who spoke to ABC News agreed Republicans lacked a clear message on affordability -- a key issue for voters. "We need to talk about pocketbook issues. We didn’t do that,” said Sarah Chamberlain, president and CEO of the Republican Main Street Partnership, a group that fundraises for moderate Republicans. Mike Blake/Reuters - PHOTO: Supporters react at a midterm election night party for Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton in Garden Grove, Calif., Nov. 3, 2026. T.W. Arrighi, a Republican strategist who worked on Republican Darline Graham’s Senate race, said Democrats were talking about affordability "in a more tangible way than we were … We have conservative solutions to these issues, we just didn’t deliver." A GOP strategist involved in many 2026 races said the party's turnout operation will likely take much of the blame. ABC News' analysis of early voting in Texas and Georgia a week before Election Day showed greater Democratic enthusiasm. "We just weren't hitting the numbers we needed to hit of just sheer Republicans voting. A lot of them stayed home, and we knew that was happening," the strategist said. Tom Brenner/Getty Images - PHOTO: Attendees react to election results confirming the results projecting Texas Democratic Senate candidate, State Rep. James Talarico as the winner during a midterm election night watch party, Nov. 3, 2026, in Washington, D.C. The Republican consultant who worked on races out West added that Republicans had "no choice" but to run on culture war issues because of the high costs brought on by the Iran war. "You can't tell people to ignore your lying eyes,” the source said. "[Republicans] had no choice but to go down the culture-war road because we couldn't talk about the economy." Trump said in a phone interview with Fox News on election night that he was "a little bit surprised" by the midterm results and added that part of the reason was the Iran war, directly linking it to gas prices. In a social media post after the election, Trump wrote that Republicans would have been more successful had he been on the ballot. Revers a l a m ong L a tino voters According to the ABC News Voter Poll, in 2026, Latino voters nationally supported Democratic House candidates by a 30-point margin. In 2024, it was a 13-point margin. Trump acknowledged his mass-deportation policies may have been "too tough" in an interview with CBS News' "60 Minutes" after the midterms. Mike Madrid, a GOP consultant who studies Latino voting behavior, said "there is no question that the ICE stuff and deportations played a role." "There’s also no question that the economy was the No. 1 factor. But in some districts, like south Texas, they're one and the same. Immigration is the economy there," Madrid said. Latino vote helped thwart Texas Republicans' redistricting effort Democrats swept every congressional district along the southern border, flipping several Republican-held seats in Texas. Billionaire donor John Catsimatidis told ABC News that the losses came down to the war in Iran and "ICE being too tough on waiters and busboys." Immigration enforcement under the Trump administration has reached local businesses and restaurants. A BC News reported l a st M a y that in D.C., federal law enforcement officials visited dozens of restaurants, carry-out spots and bars across several neighborhoods. A fight over who le a ds the RNC RNC Co-Chair KC Crosbie announced on Nov. 5 that she's challenging RNC Chair Joe Gruters, saying the party should "be willing to confront where we fell short." A source close to Gruters confirmed to ABC News that he is running for reelection. Alex Wong/Getty Images - PHOTO: Republican National Committee (RNC) Chairman Joe Gruters uses a giant gavel to mark the start of the second day of the 2026 Republican National Convention at the American Airlines Center, Sept. 10, 2026, in Dallas. While Trump has since reaffirmed his support for Gruters, some Republicans questioned Gruters' competence. “Joe Gruters failed the Republican Party, and I find it puzzling that he believes he deserves to be reelected,” said an RNC member. Florida GOP Chairman Evan Power said in a statement, however, that "Gruters was a key partner in our fight to keep the Free State of Florida red, and he’s the leader I trust to keep our party on offense and ready to win in 2028." McDaniel said "the committee should support whoever the president wants to be the RNC chair." She added that donors who may be discouraged from giving in the future need an autopsy from the party over what went wrong. "People are still wondering what happened, and the sooner that a plan is put forward, and they get in the field and they get data … That's going to be what’s going to bring donors back. But right now, I think everybody's shell-shocked." The ro a d to 2028 While Vance hasn't ruled out a run in 2028, some donors told ABC News that his proximity to Trump may be a liability. But a Vance ally who spoke to ABC News cautioned against writing off Vance, comparing it to the 2016 and 2024 election cycles, when different parts of the Republican Party wrote Trump off. Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo - PHOTO: Vice President JD Vance speaks during a National Veterans' Small Business Week event, Nov. 9, 2026, in Washington. And although Vance is still undecided about a 2028 presidential run, many of Vance's allies expect that he will run for president in 2028, sources confirmed to ABC News Chief Washington Correspondent Jonathan Karl. Vance's allies say he will decide whether to pursue a White House bid on his own timeline. But some Republicans see an opening for Secretary of State Marco Rubio to run for president in 2028 following the midterm elections. Rubio has said he has no plans to run for president in 2028, adding that he would support Vance if he mounted a presidential run. Catsimatidis said his family has been supporters of Vance, but he has known Rubio for 15 years and considers the nomination "still open." A Texas-based GOP donor said the next nominee must appeal to "most all Republicans, a majority of independents and a reasonable group of conservative Democrats." "We're in like stage two with a five-stage model of grief or something. We're not at the writing-checks-for-new-people yet stage," said one donor. "America doesn't want more MAGA." articles.title: California sues OpenAI, alleging it endangered the public by building AI without safeguards
articles.summary: OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman speaks at an event in San Francisco. (Heather Diehl / Getty Images) California sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging it failed to rein in powerful, potentially dangerous artificial intelligence technology. California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta’s office said the San Francisco-based company behind ChatGPT “misled and endangered the public by knowingly developing and testing advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect the public.” Bonta’s office alleged that an AI attack in July — in which OpenAI models broke out of an offline space , connected to the internet and hacked into Hugging Face, a rival AI company — was “entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s choice to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight.” OpenAI spokesman Drew Pusateri said in a statement to The Times that the lawsuit “appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.” He said the company has “undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity” since the Hugging Face incident, including by strengthening safeguards across its systems and creating a “framework for additional identification and disclosure” of unintended activity, and will “continue to engage” with Bonta’s office “to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.” The company previously called the Hugging Face attack a “warning shot” and pledged to make investments to prevent similar incidents. Bonta’s office said the company’s “disregard for the public safety” created a “public nuisance”  in violation of a law prohibiting businesses from engaging in “unfair” or “fraudulent” practices. “While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability,” Bonta said. The lawsuit directly challenges a rapidly growing industry that has been a massive economic boon to the state . An August report found that in 2026, California attracted $366 billion in industry-related venture capital — about 90% of all venture capital in the U.S., and three times more than every other state combined. The funding — half of it linked to just two companies, Anthropic and OpenAI — helped the state move from a multibillion-dollar fiscal deficit to a multibillion-dollar surplus, according to budget projections. The lawsuit also follows a public reckoning in recent months over claims from industry insiders that AI technology is developing too rapidly and poses an existential threat to human society. OpenAI has suggested in the past that one of the better ways to ensure AI is safe is to release it broadly. Chief Executive Sam Altman and Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki once wrote on their company’s website that its “first commitment is to build AI in service of humanity” and in a way that empowers “people broadly,” not just a concentrated few. “We believe the safer future is one where power is broadly distributed, so more of the world can participate in building a resilience ecosystem,” they wrote. They went on to say that “AI resilience refers to the collective organizations, systems, and individuals that society could put in place to anticipate, withstand, adapt to, and rapidly recover from AI-driven disruptions.” They compare building AI safeguards to making automobiles safer by improving road infrastructure and enforcing seat belt and traffic laws. “The goal wasn’t to stop people from driving — it was to make a powerful technology resilient enough for widespread use,” they wrote. The company called the Hugging Face attack  “evidence that, without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls, collaborate through unapproved channels, and take dangerous actions that no human directed.” Bonta announced a formal investigation into the Hugging Face attack and served the company with an investigative subpoena in September — part of a broader probe of mounting cybersecurity incidents involving OpenAI, Bonta’s office said. On Monday, his office said such attacks “may just be the tip of the iceberg,” but the scope of the problem isn’t fully known because OpenAI hasn’t answered “detailed questions” about them. In its own review of the Hugging Face hack alongside third-party auditors, OpenAI found that more than 700 AI agents began coordinating with each other via thousands of messages to escape containment and begin the unsanctioned attack. Subsequent investigations revealed similar testing of unreleased AI models had resulted in other cyberattacks, including on Wikipedia and government websites — sparking fears that future hacks could undermine increasingly critical infrastructure. Earlier this year, Trump signed a voluntary safety-standards accord with AI executives to establish AI protocols. California has gone further, passing more than two dozen AI-related bills, including measures that establish a state framework for independent AI safety auditors . Separate from the case in California, OpenAI announced Monday that it will allow four independent third-party evaluators to monitor how its systems behave as they are tested ahead of public release. “This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated,” OpenAI said in a statement. Bonta said Monday that securing public safety will require litigation and legislation in all 50 states and at the federal and international levels — and that he refused to accept that society should “pass off the blame to machines” while letting those who create them escape accountability. “The people who created, who create, and operate these machines need to accept the responsibility for their actions,” Bonta said at a news conference Monday. “Whether it’s a car or a toy, the law is simple: Don’t build or test things that can hurt people without proper safeguards,” he said. Bonta’s office said it is encouraging “anyone with information relevant to this case” to contact it at oag.ca.gov/report . He said his office is also watching other AI companies “closely,” but declined to elaborate. Sign up for Essential California for news, features and recommendations from the L.A. Times and beyond in your inbox six days a week. This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times . articles.title: Poll shows that 35% of Trump voters skipped the midterms
articles.summary: President Donald Trump (AP) New survey results show that 35% of President Donald Trump's 2024 voters didn't cast a ballot in the midterm elections. The findings suggest Republicans' crushing losses this month were driven largely by Trump supporters staying home rather than abandoning the GOP for Democrats, according to a new J.L. Partners analysis reported by the New York Post . The pollster found that low Republican turnout accounted for 10 percentage points of the 15-point swing toward Democrats since 2024, while voters switching parties accounted for the remaining five points. Just 8% of Trump's 2024 supporters voted for Democrats on Nov. 3. "The GOP should not throw the MAGA baby out with the bathwater just yet," J.L. Partners founding director James Johnson said, the Post reported. "If Republicans can energize their 2024 vote in 2028, then they may yet have a shot at winning again." The analysis, based on an Election Day survey of 1,000 registered voters and more than 30,000 campaign interviews, found particularly steep turnout declines among key segments of Trump's coalition. Among his 2024 supporters, 46% of those without college degrees failed to vote, along with 44% of those older than 65 and 39% of rural voters. Johnson said the turnout collapse alone would have cost Republicans control of Congress, even without voters switching parties. "Even without a single voter switching, the GOP would have lost the Senate and House," Johnson said. The findings bolster Trump's argument that Republicans suffered because he wasn't on the ballot. However, Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis suggested GOP voters stayed home because they were dissatisfied with congressional Republicans' performance. "A lot of our voters who stayed home, they stayed home because they were frustrated with the lack of productivity from Republicans in the House and Senate," DeSantis told Fox News. The survey also found potential vulnerabilities for Democrats heading into 2028. Nearly half of Democrat voters, 48%, said their midterm vote was primarily against Trump rather than in support of Democrat policies. Only 30% of registered voters believed Democrats have a viable presidential candidate for 2028. Meanwhile, CNN reported that Trump's declining popularity remains a significant obstacle for Republicans. CNN's voter polling found that 86% of Americans who disapproved of Trump's performance backed Democrats in House races. Cost of living emerged as the leading concern across every demographic group in the J.L. Partners survey. Johnson suggested the Iran war contributed to voter frustration over rising prices, particularly gasoline. The survey's overall margin of error was 3.4 percentage points. Despite the GOP's losses, Johnson said the results indicate Republicans could rebound by rebuilding turnout among Trump's 2024 supporters rather than abandoning the political coalition that returned him to the White House. © 2026 Newsmax. articles.title: 巴菲特感恩节再捐股55亿美元，这次的信只写了250字
articles.summary: 96岁的巴菲特以最简短的篇幅，完成了迄今最大规模的一次感恩节捐赠。 据周一发布的新闻稿， 沃伦·巴菲特向其家族旗下四家基金会捐赠了价值约55亿美元的伯克希尔·哈撒韦股票，捐赠规模较去年同期大幅跃升。这 是他加速财富分配计划的最新一步——他已公开承诺，将在2034年前通过三名子女将逾1600亿美元的伯克希尔资产悉数用于公益事业。 与上述捐赠规模形成鲜明对比的，是这封感恩节信的篇幅：不足250字，仅为去年逾3500字信件的零头。巴菲特在信中解释，由于9月刚就卸任伯克希尔董事长一事向股东做过详细说明，本次将"长话短说"。信中核心思想只有一句话： 善意不仅没有成本，还会以"比查理和我买过的任何东西都更好的速度"实现复利增长——这里的查理，指的是他已故的商业伙伴查理·芒格。 捐赠规模：从13.5亿到55亿 此次捐赠的股份总量为9,225,000股伯克希尔B类股。其中，以其已故妻子命名的Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation获配3,690,000股，其余三家子女基金会——The Sherwood Foundation、The Howard G. Buffett Foundation及NoVo Foundation——各获配1,845,000股。 相比之下，巴菲特去年向同四家基金会合计捐赠的股票价值约为13.5亿美元。今年的捐赠规模约为去年的四倍，体现了他"加速分配"的明确意图。 截至目前，巴菲特已累计捐出约62%的伯克希尔持股。若他选择留存这些股票，以当前市值估算，这部分股份约价值2600亿美元，届时其个人净资产将超过4200亿美元，成为仅次于埃隆·马斯克的全球第二大富豪。 伯克希尔股价：年内涨逾19%，大幅跑赢标普500 今年以来，伯克希尔股价累计上涨逾19%，创下每股超过593美元的历史新高，市值接近1.3万亿美元，同期标普500指数涨幅约为10%，伯克希尔表现明显领先大盘。 巴菲特已于去年底正式卸任伯克希尔CEO一职，由Greg Abel接掌公司领导权。今年9月，他又辞去董事长职务，就此结束长达六十余年的掌舵生涯，并在辞职信中详述了这一决定背后的考量。 250字的信：善意也有复利 尽管捐赠金额创下新高，巴菲特这次留给外界的文字却出奇地少。他在信中写道，去年感恩节他提到"善意没有成本，却无价"，而今年他只想补充一点："它会复利增长，而且速度比查理和我买过的任何东西都要快。" 他将这种"无法量化的无成本收益"归因于Benjamin Graham、Tom Murphy等师长与导师的影响，认为正是这些人的慷慨付出，使他与芒格不仅实现了巨大的物质成功，也得以将所受惠泽继续传递下去。 信的结尾，他以一贯简练的风格写道： "这个感恩节，感谢你生命中那些无私的人。更好的做法是，成为别人生命中的恩人。" 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 声网营收增长19%，但对话式AI尚未形成规模效应拖累毛利率
articles.summary: 声网的AI业务开始贡献更多收入，盈利改善仍需等待规模效应。 北京时间11月17日，声网（NASDAQ：API）发布2026年第三季度财报，营收4210万美元，同比增长19%；净利润约300万美元，同比增长10.4%。 同期，毛利率由上年同期的66%降至63.4%，经营亏损约150万美元，上年同期为160万美元。公司将毛利率下降归因于产品结构变化，其中对话式AI产品仍处于规模化前期。 这家实时音视频服务商正在将业务从人与人的通话，扩展至人与AI的互动。声网向开发者提供语音、视频和直播等能力，客户可以将其嵌入自己的应用，按实际使用量付费。客户产品中的互动越频繁、使用时间越长，就可能为声网带来更多收入。 对话式AI沿用了这套业务逻辑。企业可以接入大模型、语音识别和语音合成服务，由声网协调实时传输和对话过程，处理噪声、回声以及用户中途插话等问题。这类能力可以用于AI客服、口语教学和陪伴设备，决定了用户能否与AI流畅交流。 据业绩电话会披露，公司目前每天承载超过100万次智能体通话，需求涉及呼叫中心、陪伴等场景。管理层表示，客户越来越关注AI智能体能否在实际业务中稳定工作，企业采用也取决于交互质量和业务执行效果。 存量客户的支出已出现改善。 第三季度，声网美元计价口径下的净留存率升至110%，上年同期为97%。按公司定义，这意味着过去12个月内同一批客户的支出同比增长约10%，其中中国业务口径剔除了部分停止销售的产品。 公司称，直播电商、社交直播的扩张，以及对话式AI产品的采用，共同推动了收入增长。 新业务也增加了成本。第三季度收入成本同比增长27.9%，快于营收增速，主要来自带宽、服务器及对话式AI相关支出。研发费用同比增长14.6%至1580万美元，公司称增长主要用于对话式AI产品投入。 管理层在电话会上解释，对话式AI业务的资源利用率和部署基础设施仍有优化空间，毛利率达到目标水平可能需要数个季度。 公司还需要投入研发，并增加与客户共同推进项目落地的工程人员。管理层将2027年下半年视为实现美国通用会计准则下经营盈亏平衡的合理目标。 目前，净利润仍获得非经营收益支持。三季度，公司利息收入约360万美元、投资收益约130万美元，经营层面则继续亏损。因此，收入扩张能否覆盖技术和交付成本，将直接影响主营业务的盈利进度。 对于第四季度，声网预计营收为4400万至4500万美元，同比增长15.3%至17.9%。首席财务官王靖波在电话会上表示，公司有信心将对话式AI业务的收入贡献推向总营收的5%左右。 按上述指引粗算，对话式AI单季收入对应约220万至225万美元，商业化规模仍然较小。 管理层预计，明年这项业务的收入贡献将显著提高，但技术进步、客户采用和市场拓展仍存在不确定性，目前尚未给出明确的2027年数字指引。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: AI答案越来越多，知乎继续押注专业作者
articles.summary: 知乎把论文阅读与社区讨论连接了起来。 近日，2026知乎科学季收官。除了邀请科研人员参与线下交流，知乎还在科学季期间推出“Paper开源计划”，将论文关联、讨论入口和研究者身份绑定纳入社区功能。 基于这项计划。用户阅读论文时，可以通过插件查看知乎上的相关讨论；社区问题可以关联论文卡片，方便读者查阅原始研究；科研创作者则可绑定研究者标识ORCID，关联自己的学术身份。这些功能让论文、作者和讨论之间有了更直接的联系。 知乎也在尝试改变科学内容的呈现方式。此次科学季联合科普中国开展“AI科学创新工坊”，支持创作者将科学概念制作成交互式应用，让读者通过操作理解原理。论文讨论与交互作品，分别承接了深入交流和知识理解的需求。 这些动作背后，是知识获取方式的变化。AI搜索可以直接整合信息、生成答案，用户未必还会进入内容来源网站。 Pew在2025年发布的一项研究中，分析了900名美国成年人的浏览行为。发现出现AI摘要的谷歌搜索访问中，用户点击传统搜索结果链接的比例为8%，没有AI摘要时则为15%。 这一现象提示内容平台，原创内容被使用，并不必然带来访问和互动。对于依赖作者持续贡献内容的知识社区，用户留在什么地方阅读、向谁提问，会影响专业作者获得反馈的机会，也关系到平台能否维持活跃的讨论。 从这个角度看，知乎连接论文与社区，是在为用户回访增加具体入口。读者既能查阅研究来源，也能围绕同一篇论文继续追问。 平台上半年的专业认证调整也沿着这一方向展开，新增了科研成果、开源技术项目等认证类别，帮助识别具有专业经验的创作者。 不过，来源清楚只是交流的起点。作者对方法的解释、同行对结论的质疑，以及研究进展的后续更新，才可能让读者获得摘要之外的信息。 论文链接和身份关联提供了工具，这些内容仍需要专业作者持续参与，并由平台通过内容分发和创作激励支持其长期积累。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 逼近3800！黄金：令人疲惫的震荡区间，反弹窗口何时打开？
articles.summary: 近期黄金持续承压，从4100美元/盎司上方持续回落，一度跌至3850美元/盎司附近，周跌幅约5%，创下今年3月下旬以来的最差单周表现。压制因素较为清晰：美国通胀连续第三个月超出预期，美联储官员释放鹰派信号，交易员进一步加大加息押注，并开始消化12月加息25bp甚至50bp的可能性。 但市场异常同样明显。尽管金价跌破关键趋势水平，ETF持仓仍未出现大规模赎回，在经历前期短暂流出后，上周黄金ETF录得7.102亿美元净流入。CTA黄金仓位估算为历史最大仓位的-39%，显示算法卖压已大幅释放；非商业净多头处于多年低位，空头平均持仓规模异常低，表明空头仍具潜在增仓空间。 与此同时，黄金实物市场与官方部门的需求依然表现强劲，现货买盘在低位不断承接抛压。中国央行连续24个月增持黄金，单月增持83万盎司，中国和印度零售与官方需求继续提供支撑。 在此持仓结构下，市场关注点已从算法卖压转向技术破位后的止损压力。通常金价跌破长期牛市趋势线会触发趋势追踪资金的连锁止损与多头踩踏；但近期跌破趋势线后并未出现明显止损盘，这一关键结构信号印证长期持有者卖出枯竭。ETF持仓粘性由此成为黄金的核心缓冲，但若市场情绪持续恶化，也可能演变为最大尾部风险。 而且CME未平仓合约增幅已超出仅由CTA调仓所能解释的水平，同时期现价差下降，指向主观空头或已开始进入市场。这一结构变化表明，当前实物买盘不足以抵消空头建仓。若后续主观空头继续增仓而ETF未出现配合性抛售，空头增仓本身可能强化未来回补压力，进而形成熊陷阱。 筹码结构重构与空头博弈下的熊陷阱风险

articles.summary: AI基础设施设备商仍在享受历史罕见的繁荣。10月底，数据中心电力与散热设备龙头Vertiv交出漂亮的三季报：收入同比增长61%，有机订单增长超过100%，调整后营业利润率达到25.2%。Eaton、GE Vernova等企业的订单同样强劲。过去几年，云厂商不惜代价争抢算力建设窗口，电力、制冷和配套设备的交付能力成为稀缺资源，制造商得以同时享受收入增长、产品溢价与规模效应。 然而，11月的几件事情让这场繁荣的持续性受到更多审视。美国中期选举之后，数据中心电价、资源消耗和地方审批成为更加敏感的公共议题；英伟达创始人黄仁勋辞去CEO职务，长期担任CFO的Colette Kress出任临时CEO，也促使市场重新审视产业链核心企业对客户的融资支持。 这几件事情可能通过同一条链条相互作用。需求端的资金、电力和审批限制影响项目落地，供给端却仍在增加生产能力。如果订单增长放缓与新产能投产相遇，原本供不应求的市场就可能发生变化。日前，JP Morgan一位完整经历了科网泡沫的资深分析师Julian Mitchell已提出预警：2027年其覆盖的电气、供电、制冷设备商收入仍可能高速增长，但新增订单可能先行减速，前期扩张的产能反而会压制未来定价。 在当前时点，投资者需要重新追问：今天AI设备商令人艳羡的利润，有多少来自竞争者难以复制的技术，又有多少来自暂时缺货？ 01 高利润的另一面，是一场扩产竞赛 一家工业设备企业的超额利润，大致可能来自核心技术、可靠性与客户认证，也可能来自生产组织、及时交付和阶段性的供给短缺。现实中它们往往交织在一起。尤其当需求突然爆发，率先具备量产能力的企业可以获得近似技术垄断的定价权，却未必真正掌握不可复制的工艺。订单和利润率能够证明企业当前竞争力很强，却还不足以证明这种优势能维持十年。 ……

articles.title: AI暴跌前，华尔街大佬分道扬镳：桥水、索罗斯Q3大砍英伟达持仓，”木头姐“、Tepper逆势加码，德鲁肯米勒清仓闪迪、台积电
articles.summary: 随着2026年三季度13F文件集中披露，全球顶级投资机构的持仓调整路径浮出水面——英伟达遭遇机构史上罕见的大分流，桥水转向AI硬件产业链，索罗斯完成"芯片内部换仓"，Druckenmiller大举清仓半导体并转向黄金与SpaceX，伯克希尔则继续远离科技追逐，坚守地产与航空。 这批截至9月30日的持仓报告， 恰好卡在一个高度敏感的时间节点： 英伟达CEO黄仁勋于11月12日被董事会解除职务，股价随之剧烈波动。而这一切，均发生在三季度持仓数据所反映的时间窗口之后。据holdingsintel.com汇总的497家机构13F数据， 英伟达成为本季度分歧最大的单一标的 ——减持方阵容包括Sixth Street Partners清仓1.6亿股、文艺复兴科技减持99.7%，加仓方则有ARK增持85%、DekaBank增持648%，Tepper亦增持。 此外，13F报告显示，Ken Griffin旗下的城堡投资（Citadel Advisors）组合中对英伟达的权重小幅下降了约1.31%（持股变动约减少117万股），同期其持仓市值约为27亿美元，占组合比例约1.46%。 在英伟达之外，多条隐藏主线同步浮现：ARK、Druckenmiller、Tepper均在三季度新建或加仓SpaceX； “减算力、加存储/设备”成为隐性主线 ，桥水买入应用材料、美光，索罗斯买入SK海力士，Druckenmiller转向希捷与西部数据；伯克希尔则以96亿美元回购自家股票，继续以现金和耐心对抗市场喧嚣。 桥水：减科技巨头，加AI硬件产业链 据 华尔街见闻文章 写道，桥水联合基金三季度披露的974项投资头寸总市值达230亿美元，本季度持仓重塑方向高度清晰： 削减科技巨头与标普ETF，将资金转向AI芯片硬件、存储及能源板块 。 增持方面 ，高通持仓从16.2万股增至87.8万股，增幅约440%，对应市值增加约1.32亿美元；AppLovin A类股增持53.6万股至68.3万股，市值增加约1.23亿美元；存储芯片方向同样获得显著增持，美光持仓增加12万股至23.7万股，市值增加约1.18亿美元；闪迪增持6.6万股至6.68万股，市值增加约1.15亿美元。此外，射频芯片公司Qorvo本季度增持逾103.7万股，持股总量达106.8万股。 减持方面 ，道富标普500 ETF持仓减少近191.7万股，市值减少约13.78亿美元；iShares Core S&P 500 ETF同步削减149.4万股，市值减少约10.93亿美元。个股层面，Alphabet A类股持仓减少86.2万股，市值减少约3.14亿美元；亚马逊持仓减少105.5万股，市值减少约2.41亿美元；微软减持幅度约69%。 尽管如此， 英伟达仍以6.14亿美元市值位列桥水前五大重仓股第三位 ，持股268.8万股，季内减持约117.8万股，降幅约30%，仍为组合中半导体标的中最重要的单一持仓。博通以4.62亿美元紧随其后，持仓几乎维持不变。 工业板块是本季度持仓权重降幅最大的板块，桥水完全退出联合太平洋铁路（减少51.4万股，市值减少约1.40亿美元）和卡车制造商Paccar。能源方向，桥水新建西方石油仓位155万股，市值约8577万美元，并新买入电力公司Dominion Energy约151.6万股。 索罗斯：减英伟达，大举买入英特尔与SK海力士 据 华尔街见闻文章 提及，据彭博对季度监管文件的汇编数据，乔治·索罗斯的同名家族办公室在截至9月30日的季度内 将英伟达持仓削减近五分之一 ，这是该机构今年首次披露的减仓操作，此前其一直在增持该股。 具体而言，索罗斯基金管理公司上季度出售了约20.6万股英伟达股份，按当时股价计算市值最高达4740万美元，截至9月30日其剩余英伟达持仓价值接近2亿美元。与此同时，英伟达看跌期权也从40万股减至35万股。 然而，这并非单纯的"减科技"操作，而是一次 芯片内部的方向性切换 。索罗斯将英特尔持仓从10万股大幅增至283万股，增幅约28倍，市值约3.4亿美元，成为该基金最大单一股票持仓；同期新建仓SK海力士ADR 32.5万股；Meta增持近6倍。整体逻辑指向：减"贵的算力"，加"便宜的逻辑芯片和存储"。 宏观对冲方面，索罗斯将能源精选SPDR的看跌期权从200万股底层股份增至1090万股（名义价值约6.7亿美元），并新增约3.28亿美元的油气勘探ETF看跌期权，合计约10亿美元名义空头对冲。同时买入长期美债（TLT）看涨期权约2.37亿美元及公用事业（XLU）看涨期权约2.15亿美元。 据彭博亿万富翁指数，现年96岁的索罗斯身家为97亿美元，其基金由前瑞银集团高管Dawn Fitzpatrick主导。 Druckenmiller：清芯片、买黄金，试水SpaceX 据 华尔街见闻文章 写道，传奇投资者Stanley Druckenmiller在2026年三季度对旗下Duquesne家族办公室投资组合进行了大幅调仓， 清仓多只半导体及科技巨头股票，同时新建仓SpaceX、Palantir等标的，并转向黄金矿业板块 。 清仓与大幅减仓方面，Druckenmiller完全退出AMD（72,900股）、闪迪（34,900股）和Alphabet A类股（336,300股）。台积电是削减幅度最大的标的，持仓从589,700股骤降至32,700股， 降幅达94% ，市值仅剩约1,490万美元。STMicroelectronics持仓从310万股减至162万股，降幅约48%；CRH持仓降幅约71%。此外，联合航空（794,800股）、达美航空、DR Horton，以及标普500和罗素2000指数的看涨期权头寸均被悉数清出。整体来看，此次调仓共涉及退出约48个持仓。 新建仓方面，Druckenmiller买入SpaceX 202,125股（约3050万美元）、Palantir 80,100股、AppLovin 109,460股。 黄金矿业板块获得集中布局 ：新建仓纽蒙特黄金公司Newmont 380,400股（市值约4,390万美元）、Barrick Mining 1,050,000股（市值约4,290万美元）以及Agnico Eagle，三只金矿股合计建仓约1.29亿美元。 值得关注的是，Druckenmiller在清仓台积电、AMD、闪迪的同时，却大幅增持存储硬件方向—— 希捷科技持仓增至341,800股，市值约3.152亿美元，升为第二大重仓股 ，并增持180%；同时新建仓TTM Technologies及西部数据。这并非逃离科技，而是从高估值算力芯片切向存储和更便宜的硬件。 从当前持仓结构来看，临床基因检测平台公司Natera为第一大重仓股，占整体约44.7亿美元投资组合的29.2%，集中度极高。据彭博亿万富翁指数，Druckenmiller净资产约为125亿美元。 伯克希尔：远离科技喧嚣，押注地产、航空与"App翻新工厂" 据 华尔街见闻文章 写道，在格雷格·阿贝尔（Greg Abel）接棒巴菲特掌舵的第三个完整季度，伯克希尔·哈撒韦操作依旧克制：新建仓1只、加仓4只、减仓6只，未清仓任何标的，换手率仅3.33%。 增持方向高度集中于住宅建筑和航空 。房屋建筑商Lennar A类股从1311.17万股增至2603.44万股，增幅达98.6%，持仓规模接近翻倍；B类股同步从29.81万股增至55.30万股，增幅约85.5%。达美航空连续第三个季度获加仓，持股从5732万股增至6445万股，增幅约12.4%，新增持仓价值约6.2亿美元。 本季度最引人注目的新仓位是意大利科技公司Bending Spoons（BSP） ，截至9月30日持有约2069万股，披露市值约6.89亿美元。这家公司专门收购"有用户、但增长放缓"的过气软件并加以改造，旗下资产包括AOL、Vimeo、Evernote、Eventbrite、WeTransfer等知名互联网产品。伯克希尔在其7月IPO时投入约6亿美元，10月又追加3.3亿美元，两笔合计约9.3亿美元。 减持方面，Capital One持仓从300万股减至115万股，降幅约61.7%；VeriSign持仓从898.99万股降至592.21万股，降幅约34.1%；美国银行持仓减少约2753万股，降幅约5.7%，对应市值约15亿美元；Kroger降幅约10.3%。 从资本配置全貌来看， 伯克希尔三季度回购自家股票约96亿美元，而买卖外部股票几乎打平（买入23.7亿美元、卖出27.9亿美元） 。截至9月30日，公司持有的现金、现金等价物及美国国债约3523亿美元。苹果（约759亿美元）、美国运通（约462亿美元）、可口可乐（约344亿美元）、Alphabet A类股（约271亿美元）、美国银行（约248亿美元）仍构成前五大重仓。 AI“股神”、Situational Awareness基金：规模单季度缩水187亿美元 根据最新披露的13F文件，Leopold Aschenbrenner创立的Situational Awareness基金截至9月30日的申报持仓规模为15.8亿美元，而三个月前的6月30日这一数字为202.4亿美元——单季度缩水187亿美元，降幅高达92%。这份文件为此前已在市场广泛流传的爆仓事件提供了完整的书面记录。此次持仓骤降的直接诱因是7月下旬的强制平仓。 据报道，该基金的大部分公开市场持仓以约10%的折价批量出售给城堡投资（Citadel），这也在一定程度上解释了后者当月的亮眼表现。然而，清仓后不久，该基金便以几乎相同的交易逻辑重建头寸，并于9月再度遭遇重创。 文件显示，Situational Awareness原有26个持仓标的，其中21个在报告期内被完全清仓。 已关闭的头寸涵盖价值56.7亿美元的Sandisk、55.7亿美元的美光科技（Micron）、19亿美元的Bloom Energy股票、12.7亿美元的台积电（TSMC）以及12.3亿美元的Nebius。 据彭博此前报道，在爆仓事件发生逾一个月前，已有分析人士警告称，对AI相关标的使用大规模掉期杠杆可能引发类似Archegos的强制清算风险。7月下旬，风险最终兑现。 截至9月30日，当前申报持仓中约三分之二为认购期权，而非直接持股——这意味着在原有股票杠杆被强制清除后，该基金选择以期权形式重建相似敞口。 具体而言， Bloom Energy的持仓从14.58万股基础股份扩张至对应140万股的认购期权，名义价值达3.89亿美元；新增对Nebius的认购期权名义价值3.33亿美元，对Sandisk的认购期权名义价值1.83亿美元，以及对一只存储器ETF的认购期权名义价值1.4亿美元。 唯一值得注意的直接股票持仓增量来自SharonAI——持股数量较前一期增加50%至807万股，市值约4.41亿美元。 英伟达：机构史上罕见大分流 英伟达是本季度13F持仓报告里分歧最大的标的。 减持阵营 ：Sixth Street Partners清仓1.6亿股；文艺复兴科技减持99.7%，从709万股降至2.3万股；桥水减持约30%；索罗斯减持近五分之一；Druckenmiller大幅削减台积电等芯片持仓；据彭博，参与减持的家族办公室至少达十余家，但均保留了部分英伟达仓位，截至季度末合计持有的英伟达股份市值仍超过10亿美元。 加仓阵营 ：ARK增持85%，英伟达升至组合3.4%；DekaBank增持648%；David Tepper旗下Appaloosa将英伟达增持31%至200万股，芯片持仓占组合比重从35%升至39%。 值得特别关注的是，英伟达自身的13F文件显示，其英特尔持仓从2.148亿股降至1.611亿股，按季末股价计算约出售了65亿美元的英特尔股票，超过其约一年前购入该笔股份所支付的约50亿美元。与此同时，英伟达将SpaceX升为最大持仓，市值约196.8亿美元，整体13F持仓规模下降24%至483亿美元。 在芯片分歧加剧的背景下， SpaceX成为本季度又一个分歧点 。 ARK将SpaceX增持51%至10.2亿美元，升为仅次于特斯拉的第二大持仓；Druckenmiller新建仓202,125股，约3050万美元；Tepper将SpaceX持仓扩大约17倍至5.57亿美元；英伟达将SpaceX列为最大持仓，市值约196.8亿美元。 与此同时，Michael Platt旗下BlueCrest则反向操作，将SpaceX持仓削减94%，从2.42亿美元降至约1300万美元，成为少数逆势减持者。 这一分歧折射出当前市场的深层逻辑： 当AI算力交易的高度集中性引发机构分歧，商业航天作为另一条长期增长叙事，正在吸引越来越多的顶级资金悄然布局。 本季度13F文件中，一条贯穿多家机构的隐性主线值得关注： 多位大佬不约而同从英伟达代表的算力芯片，向存储和半导体设备切换 。 桥水买入美光、闪迪、高通、Qorvo；索罗斯新建仓SK海力士ADR；Druckenmiller清仓台积电、AMD、闪迪，却将希捷科技大幅加仓至第二大重仓，并新买入TTM Technologies；ARK增持AI云CoreWeave 58%。Lone Pine 清仓希捷，Tepper加仓美光。 其他机构动向 Cathie Wood的ARK ：组合规模从154亿美元增至174亿美元。英伟达增持85%；AMD砍仓52%，从组合权重约4.6%压至2.4%；SpaceX增持51%至10.2亿美元；Meta翻倍；CoreWeave增58%；稳定币公司Circle增50%；特斯拉再增22%。特斯拉加SpaceX合计占组合12.75%。Roblox被砍79%接近出清。 Bill Ackman的潘兴广场 ：总市值从255亿增至308亿美元。新建仓洲际交易所（ICE）和眼科巨头爱尔康（ALC），各约10亿美元；微软砍34.51%、Meta减11.35%；奈飞增持17.82%。 高瓴HHLR ：增持拼多多789%、阿里巴巴1,250%，两只合计占组合近四成。 段永平H&H ：总市值约172亿美元，拼多多加仓296.88万股升为第三大重仓（12.69%），特斯拉增至8.42%；英伟达减持63%，占比从6.58%降至3.08%。段永平随后公开表态"不看空但暂时也不加码"，并表示"买英伟达的大部分理由还在，只是黄仁勋不在了"，计划买回被call走的股票。 高毅资产 ：清仓英伟达、美光、闪迪，大幅加仓阿里巴巴、BOSS直聘。 风险提示及免责条款
